newsitem.title: UK: Germany's rock-bottom yields set to pick up.
newsitem.headline: Germany's rock-bottom yields set to pick up.

text.p: German bond yields are about as low as they can go, and while they are not about to rocket higher they risk a gradual pick-up, analysts said on Monday.
Key economic data out this week are unlikely to be the catalyst for a rise, but investors might find better prospects in buoyant U.S. Treasuries short-term, analysts said.
"We're not looking for anymore downward potential on German yields," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"All the factors suggest yields should be going back above six percent over the next three months."

Ten-year German bonds were yielding 5.830 percent at 1200 GMT, around the same as their late January lows for the year. Bond yields have dwindled and prices risen as the German economy has plodded along at a lethargic pace with few signs of inflation to eat into returns.

Analysts said data out later in the week might rattle the market on first reading, but were unlikely to herald a miraculous recovery in the German economy. First on the list is German M3 money supply for October.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing sounded a warning of a potentially large figure last Friday when he said the privatisation of Deutsche Telecom -- Europe's largest share flotation -- could swell the data.

Holger Farinkrug, senior economist at UBS in Frankfurt, said he raised his forecast for M3 growth to 8.8 percent from 7.9 after Issing's comments. But with a rise well-flagged and largely accounted for, the market should be able to swallow the increase. In September, M3 showed an 8.4 percent rise.
The Ifo index of German business sentiment is due on Wednesday.
Lewis said he expected a rise to 96.0 from 95.7 in October with initial government data overestimating economic weakness in September. Others saw it stagnating around current levels.
Farinkrug said: "We know new orders and output were weak in September, we know unemployment was rising strongly in October. The dollar has been declining in the second half of October."
He said recent tax discussions were not favourable for companies, further putting a damper on corporate expectations and sentiment.
"For all these reasons I would be surprised if it went up further."
While Farinkrug said there was no immediate upward pressure on German bond, or Bund, yields it would be difficult for the market to cling to levels below six percent.
"I don't see much immediate pressure but generally history has taught us levels below six percent are very hard to sustain in Germany," he said.

While the convergence of bond yields among prospective members of European economic and monetary union (EMU) has helped other markets in Europe, for Germany it could have a bearish fallout, analysts said.

The market currently had attached no risk premium to Bunds from EMU beginning on time with Italy and Spain in the starting block. But the convergence of Italian and Spanish yields on German debt should begin to take its toll on Bund yields.

Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets in London, said he believed German yields could still drop a little further with interest rates set to remain at rock bottom for some time to come, but he still favours the U.S. market.
"There is very bullish sentiment in the U.S. and Treasuries seem to want to go higher and will continue to do so at the expense of spread narrowing," he said.
"So although I think Germany can resume outperforming at some stage it's probably not the best trade to put on at the moment."
The 10-year T-note/Bund spread was at 45 basis points.
